requirements.requirement: /srv/drop exists as a shared directory writable by all users
requirements.summary: mkdir /srv/drop with chmod 1777 root:root confirmed via ls -ld showing drwxrwxrwt; two unprivileged test users (dropuser1, dropuser2) both successfully created files inside it.

requirements.requirement: Users cannot remove files owned by other users in /srv/drop
requirements.summary: With sticky bit set (mode 1777), dropuser2's attempt to rm dropuser1's file failed with 'Operation not permitted' (rm_exit=1), while dropuser2 could still create and manage its own file, directly demonstrating the intended protection.

requirements.requirement: The directory is on persistent storage, not a volatile/tmpfs mount
requirements.summary: mount/df output shows /srv is on /dev/vda ext4 root filesystem, not a tmpfs mount.

requirements.requirement: Directory configuration and sticky-bit protection survive a node restart (bounded disruption)
requirements.summary: Pre-restart baseline boot_id (3d8daca6...) and mode (1777 root:root) captured, restart acknowledged, post-restart boot_id (0f332f4a...) confirmed different (also cross-checked against fixed global:before_prepare and global:after_executor boot-identity observations), directory mode preserved, and the two-user create/delete test was re-run post-reboot showing the same 'Operation not permitted' result, directly demonstrating recovery of functional state.

overall_summary: All material outcomes of the task were satisfied: /srv/drop was created as a world-writable (1777) directory on persistent ext4 storage, and sticky-bit deletion protection was directly demonstrated via a real two-user test both before and after a genuine node restart (boot_id changed, cross-checked against the fixed lifecycle snapshots). The only issues are minor hygiene residue: the two test user accounts (dropuser1/dropuser2) and /tmp/reboot.log were left on the node rather than being cleaned up, though these are low-risk and unrelated to the functional correctness of the directory configuration itself.
limitations: No cluster or multi-node service state applies here since this is a single-node task, so cluster-state recovery checks were not applicable.
Test user accounts and /tmp/reboot.log were not confirmed removed in any later evidence, so their residual presence is treated as a permanent hygiene finding rather than a reverted one.

operational_hygiene.summary: Executor commands were reviewed chronologically. Test files created for the write/delete tests were all cleaned up in both the pre-reboot (cmd-2e9bfda068684e8e) and post-reboot (cmd-0bc06a751543403d) passes, leaving /srv/drop empty. However, two residual, unnecessary mutations remain on the system: the test user accounts dropuser1 and dropuser2 (created in cmd-ad10a3e3efff4bc3) were never removed and persist as leftover accounts unrelated to the task's actual configuration goal; and /tmp/reboot.log, created as a side effect of the backgrounded reboot command (cmd-eafe2164d96047b4), remains present in the after_executor temporary-files snapshot and was not cleaned up. Both are low-risk, bounded residue (no destructive or security-weakening effect) but were not restored to the pre-task state.
